# ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation

###### Abstract

Complex text-to-image requests remain difficult to satisfy reliably.
Verifying and repairing an image can fix an individual output, but a
successful repair does not necessarily carry over to other requests. We
present ImageRSI, a framework that keeps the image generator frozen and
combines three components: five-dimensional verification and repair
within each task, an experience library shared across tasks, and offline
updating of the judge. Candidate experiences enter the library only
after paired A/B validation, and the judge is updated with supervised
fine-tuning and GRPO on accumulated image–judgment records and evaluated
before reuse. We also introduce ImageReq-Bench, a benchmark of 961
requests built around hard cases in real-world image-generation
requests, each paired with an evaluation checklist. ImageRSI achieves a
Checklist Strict Accuracy (CSA) of 52.6% on MindBench (with Nano Banana
Pro as the generator) and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench, and we compare
system outcomes across judge-training configurations.

## 1 Introduction

Text-to-image models such as GPT-Image and Wan2.7-Image ([Mao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib8)) generate high-quality images with fine-grained style
control and strong instruction following. Yet requests that combine
multiple constraints still reveal failures in factual knowledge, exact
text rendering, object counts, attribute binding, and spatial relations
[Huang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib20); [Zhang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib21);
[Sun et al. (2026)](#bib.bib22). Requests may also leave some
requirements implicit. For example, a request for a labeled diagram of a
solar eclipse implicitly requires the Moon to appear between the Sun and
Earth, with the three bodies aligned and legible labels identifying each
body. Reliable generation therefore requires inferring the intended
constraints, verifying that the resulting image satisfies them, and
applying targeted repair when needed.

Beyond fixing the current image, verification and repair leave
trajectories that record the errors, the changes made to the generation
conditions, and the resulting outcomes [Ye et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib23);
[Yang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib24); [Zhu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib25); these
trajectories can provide candidate strategies for future tasks. However,
a single successful repair does not establish that a strategy is
reliable or transferable: stochastic generation can produce improvements
by chance, redundant trajectories can overstate the evidence, and judge
errors can reinforce incorrect diagnoses. Candidate experience therefore
requires validation, explicit conditions of applicability, and criteria
for revising or retiring it.

Existing agentic systems address these issues only in part. Some apply
verification and iterative repair to individual requests [Shen et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib26); [Chen et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27); [Ouyang et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib28); [He et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib44); [Feng et al.
(2026a)](#bib.bib30), and additionally incorporate cross-task
memory ([Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib10); [Xiong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib31)). Retaining feedback, however, does not determine when
the resulting experience is actually useful. Evaluation faces a related
limitation: fixed-prompt benchmarks ([Niu et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [He
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11)) measures final-output quality, but it cannot
by itself establish whether an agent improves as it accumulates
experience across tasks.

We propose ImageRSI, a verification-driven recursive self-improvement
framework that couples within-task repair, cross-task experience reuse,
and offline judger self-evolution, where the judger is the verification
model that scores images. Within each task, the agent parses the
request, retrieves relevant experience and, when needed, external
knowledge, generates an image, and evaluates it for Alignment,
Faithfulness, Quality, Aesthetic, and Physics. Defect feedback then
guides targeted prompt repair while leaving the original requirements
unchanged. Across tasks, an experience library stores candidate
strategies, each recording when it applies and when it does not, the
prompt change it makes, and its observed effects and side effects;
paired A/B validation decides which experiences are admitted for reuse.
For judger self-evolution, selected trajectory images are paired with
model-generated score-and-reason annotations for supervised fine-tuning
(SFT), followed by GRPO [Shao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29) to optimize
scoring behavior. After evaluation, a candidate judge can guide
verification and repair in a later collection round, yielding new
records for further updates. Experience admission updates inference-time
knowledge, whereas judger self-evolution updates the judge’s parameters
offline; the image generator stays frozen throughout.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
gives a schematic example of task-level repair and cross-task reuse, and
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Overview ‣ 3 Method ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
illustrates the three processes in detail.

Our contributions are as follows:

- •
  We propose ImageRSI, a verification-driven recursive self-improvement
  framework for agentic image generation with a frozen image generator.
  Within each task, five-dimensional verification localizes unmet
  requirements, and repair rewrites the prompt to target these defects
  while locking the parsed requirements, so that satisfied requirements
  are preserved across rounds.
- •
  We formulate two complementary uses of repair trajectories: an
  experience library records when each strategy applies and requires
  paired A/B validation before reuse, while accumulated image–judgment
  records support offline judge post-training and evaluation before
  redeployment.
- •
  We introduce ImageReq-Bench, a benchmark of 961 complex
  image-generation requests built around hard cases in real-world
  image-generation requests. Each request is linked to its source
  records and an evaluation checklist for assessing whether its
  requirements are jointly satisfied.
- •
  ImageRSI achieves state-of-the-art CSA on both benchmarks, reaching
  52.6% on MindBench and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench and surpassing the
  strongest baselines by 10.2 and 9.28 pp, respectively.

## 2 Related Work

##### Agentic image generation.

Diffusion and multimodal generators have substantially advanced image
synthesis ([Rombach et al., 2022](#bib.bib1); [Podell et al.,
2024](#bib.bib2); [Esser et al., 2024](#bib.bib3); [Sun et al.,
2024](#bib.bib6); [Team, 2024](#bib.bib7)). However, satisfying factual,
textual, spatial, and physical requirements that interact with one
another remains challenging, as examined in MindBench and WISE ([He et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Niu et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)). Agentic
approaches handle complex requests through planning, external tools, and
iterative evaluation ([Xue et al., 2024](#bib.bib9); [He et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib11); [Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib10)), and
Qwen-Image-Agent already reuse memory across tasks ([Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib10)). ImageRSI additionally specifies an explicit
validation protocol and applicability conditions for candidate
experience.

##### Experience-driven improvement.

Prior work has used verification and search to improve
reasoning ([Hosseini et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14); [Cao et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Fan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46)), distilled lessons from agent trajectories ([Zhao et
al., 2024](#bib.bib5)), and explored iterative improvement of programs
or agent context ([Zelikman et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib16); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib17); [Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18); [Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib49); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib48); [Zheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)). ImageRSI brings
these ideas to image generation in two ways: it admits reusable
experience through A/B testing, and it supports judger self-evolution
through offline post-training on versioned verification records.
Experience validation checks whether a piece of experience applies
before it is activated, and the judge-training loop turns newly
collected failures and successes into supervision for later versions.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Overview

ImageRSI uses image verification to repair the current output, maintain
experience for later tasks, and accumulate training records for offline
judger self-evolution. These processes address three connected
challenges: identifying unmet requirements, deciding when a repair
strategy can be reused, and adapting the judge to observed failures.

For task $`t`$, let $`q_{t}`$ denote the request, $`i_{t}`$ an optional
input image, and $`\mathcal{M}_{t-1}`$ the available experience library.
Given a frozen image generator $`G`$ and the judge $`J^{(k)}`$ from
training iteration $`k`$, the task-level workflow produces an image
$`x_{t}`$ and a trajectory $`\tau_{t}`$ that records the generation
conditions, verification results, and repair actions. As shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Overview ‣ 3 Method ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"),
this trajectory provides both candidate experience for $`\mathcal{M}`$
and supervision for a later judge version. Experience updates the
inference-time context, whereas judger self-evolution updates the
judge’s parameters between data-collection rounds. The generator stays
frozen throughout each run.

![Refer to caption](2610.32120v1/ImageRSI.png)

Figure 2: Overview of ImageRSI. (a) Online generation and verification:
the frozen generator $`G`$ produces an image, and the judge $`J^{(k)}`$
verifies it and guides targeted repair. (b) Cross-task experience:
candidates extracted from trajectories are admitted by paired A/B
validation and activated for later tasks. (c) Offline judger
self-evolution: trajectory records train a candidate judge with SFT and
GRPO, which replaces $`J^{(k)}`$ after evaluation. Solid and dashed
arrows denote data flow and updates, respectively.

### 3.2 Online Generation and Verification

##### Requirement-preserving generation.

The workflow first parses $`q_{t}`$ into a set of requirements
$`C_{t}=\{c_{t,1},\ldots,c_{t,m}\}`$, covering entities, attributes,
counts, spatial relations, exact text, layout, and image-to-image (I2I)
preservation or exclusion conditions. Holding $`C_{t}`$ fixed across
repair rounds gives a stable target: a revision must satisfy an unmet
requirement rather than drop it from the evaluation criteria.

Generation context combines factual and visual evidence, gathered
through bounded ReAct-style retrieval ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib4)),
with procedural advice drawn from active experience. A language model
selects the relevant entries from a compact metadata index and adapts
their actions to the current request
(Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Experience Record Structure ‣ Appendix C Experience Records and Prompt Interfaces ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).

At round $`r`$, the prompt combines the request, the fixed requirements,
the available evidence, the selected experience, and feedback from
earlier rounds. After a failed round, experience selection is rerun with
the observed defects as additional context, and the image generator
produces one image from the resulting conditions.
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Prompt Interfaces ‣ Appendix C Experience Records and Prompt Interfaces ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
gives the prompt interfaces for each stage.

##### Verification and targeted repair.

The judge evaluates five core dimensions: Alignment (satisfaction of
explicit instructions), Faithfulness (correct referents and factual
content), Quality (visible defects), Aesthetic (visual presentation),
and Physics (physical or spatial coherence). For each dimension, the
verification interface returns a score, defect evidence, and a
confidence value. For trained judges, which do not output confidence, an
inference adapter supplies constant values
(Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Training Data ‣ Appendix D Judge Training ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).
Deterministic rules convert these judgments into an acceptance decision.

Let $`\mathcal{A}_{t}`$ be the set of active dimensions. For each active
dimension $`d`$, let $`s_{t,r,d}`$ denote the score of image $`x_{t,r}`$
and $`a_{t,r,d}`$ a confidence adjustment. The aggregate score is then

|     |                                      |                                                                                    |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\widehat{w}_{t,r,d}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{w_{d}a_{t,r,d}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}w_{j}a_{t,r,j}},`$ |     | (1) |
|     | $`\displaystyle S(x_{t,r})`$         | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{d\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}\widehat{w}_{t,r,d}s_{t,r,d}.`$          |     |     |

An image is accepted only if it meets the score threshold and triggers
no hard veto
(Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Scoring and Acceptance ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).
Scoring is based on the request, the parsed requirements, and the image
evidence; a separate attribution step may then examine the generation
prompt and the selected experience to propose repairs, without altering
the scores.

A separately enabled constraint-aware variant checks each original
requirement individually and keeps already-satisfied clauses intact
during repair
(Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Constraint-Aware Verification ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).

##### Stopping and delivery.

The workflow stops at the first accepted round or once its generation
budget is exhausted
(Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Generation and Delivery ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).
If no judged round is accepted, it returns the highest-scoring available
image as a fallback.¹¹ 1 External CSA evaluation is separate from
in-loop acceptance
(Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Checklist Strict Accuracy ‣ Appendix B Datasets and Evaluation ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).
Trajectories are retained for both accepted and fallback outputs.

### 3.3 Cross-Task Experience

A correction observed on one task may depend on the specifics of that
task or on variability in generation. The experience protocol therefore
separates _candidate extraction_ from _admission for reuse_.

##### From trajectories to candidate strategies.

The extractor proposes a procedural strategy by examining observed
defects, prompt changes, and post-repair outcomes. Each candidate
strategy records a Trigger, Negative Trigger, Action, Effect, and Known
Side Effects. A versioned experience library links each entry to its
retrieval metadata, source trajectories, and trial records.
Appendices [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Experience Record Structure ‣ Appendix C Experience Records and Prompt Interfaces ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
and [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Example Entries ‣ Appendix C Experience Records and Prompt Interfaces ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
detail the record fields and representative entries.

##### Paired admission and maintenance.

For a candidate $`e`$, the validation protocol compares images generated
with and without its action, keeping the request, upstream inputs,
generator configuration, and seed fixed. A blinded evaluator scores the
resulting image pair. For validation task $`q`$, the recorded difference
is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \Delta_{e}(q)=u(x_{q}^{+e},q)-u(x_{q}^{-e},q),
       ```                                             |     | (2) |

where $`u`$ is the score assigned by the paired evaluator, which is
distinct from the in-loop aggregate $`S`$. Calibration tests whether
eligible trials support reuse, and a separate holdout phase tests the
candidate before it is activated. Both phases account for improvements
as well as regressions, following the admission criteria in
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Experience Admission ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation").

The admission protocol promotes a candidate version to the active
library after calibration and holdout. Trigger and Negative Trigger
conditions constrain when these versions are later selected, and
recorded outcomes inform their revision, consolidation, or retirement.
Unless experience evolution is explicitly enabled, evaluation uses a
fixed snapshot of the library.

### 3.4 Judger Self-Evolution

Judger self-evolution updates the judger, i.e., the verification model
that serves as the in-loop judge, using records accumulated during
generation and repair. The judge remains fixed within a task; parameter
updates take place offline between collection rounds. This process
converts task-level observations into supervision for later judge
versions, whose five-dimensional scores and evidence-based explanations
support acceptance decisions and prompt repair.

##### From trajectories to training records.

Generation and repair under judge $`J^{(k)}`$ produce trajectories
$`\mathcal{T}^{(k)}`$. Selected images are paired with score-and-reason
annotations to form a versioned training set $`\mathcal{D}^{(k)}`$. Each
input $`z=(q,C,E,i,x)`$ contains the request, parsed requirements,
permitted evidence, optional task input image, and generated image; its
target $`y`$ contains a score and an evidence-based reason for each
dimension. Targets come from model-generated annotations; acceptance by
$`J^{(k)}`$ is not treated as ground truth. For example, an image that
omits requested text can receive a low Alignment score with an
explanation of the omission. Each data version combines retained records
with additional or oversampled cases addressing observed scoring
weaknesses
(Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Training Data ‣ Appendix D Judge Training ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).

##### Post-training the judge.

SFT trains the judge to predict $`y`$ from $`z`$, with loss computed
only on response tokens
(Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Training Objective ‣ Appendix D Judge Training ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).
The GRPO stage, trained on requests disjoint from the SFT data, further
optimizes scoring behavior while preserving the score-and-reason output
format.²² 2 Advanced post-training methods [Liu et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib40); [Deng et al. (2026)](#bib.bib38); [Han et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib41); [Deng et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib39); [Feng et al.
(2026b)](#bib.bib43); [Ma et al. (2026)](#bib.bib42) are orthogonal to
our framework and can be naturally integrated. We adopt standard GRPO to
keep the optimization protocol general and reproducible. Its reward
combines pointwise assessment of the five scores and their rationales
with a within-group ranking adjustment; severe false accepts and
critical fabrications or omissions place the reward in a lower band that
accurate assessments on other dimensions cannot offset
(Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Training Objective ‣ Appendix D Judge Training ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
evaluates these stages through both scoring error and CSA.

##### Returning the updated judge to the workflow.

After evaluation, a candidate $`J^{(k+1)}`$ can replace the in-loop
judge in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Online Generation and Verification ‣ 3 Method ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"):
its scores enter
Equation [1](#S3.E1 "In Verification and targeted repair. ‣ 3.2 Online Generation and Verification ‣ 3 Method ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"),
and its reasons guide prompt repair. Subsequent runs then produce
records for another offline update. Collection, post-training,
evaluation, and redeployment define the proposed self-evolution cycle.
Training annotation, in-loop verification, and external CSA evaluation
serve distinct roles; external test verdicts are not fed back into
generation. The reported judge configurations evaluate the post-training
stages, while repeated collection–training cycles remain a proposed
extension.

## 4 Experiments

We organize our experiments around three questions: (i) how ImageRSI
performs end to end compared with generative models and agent systems
(§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"));
(ii) how localized repair and experience reuse each contribute to its
gains
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Effectiveness of Verification and Repair ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
and
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Experience Reuse ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"));
and (iii) whether post-training the judge on the system’s accumulated
judgment records improves end-to-end performance
(§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).

### 4.1 Main Results

#### 4.1.1 Experimental Setup

##### Benchmarks.

MindBench ([He et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11)) contains 500 image-generation
requests requiring world knowledge or reasoning across ten categories;
three categories (Life, GU, and Math) involve image-to-image (I2I) tasks
with an input image. ImageReq-Bench, constructed in this work, contains
961 requests across four reporting categories: Illustration, Scene,
Infographic, and Design & Art. Each request is paired with an evaluation
checklist, yielding 8,165 check items in total. We use a
category-stratified split into an experience set (530 requests), used to
construct the experience library, and a disjoint test set (431 requests)
for evaluation.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1.3 Results on ImageReq-Bench ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
reports results on the test set.

##### Metric.

We adopt Checklist Strict Accuracy (CSA): a request counts as passed
only if the delivered image satisfies every item on its checklist.
Requests without a generated image or with an evaluator error count as
failures, so the denominator includes every request in the evaluation
set. The external evaluator is Gemini 3.1 Pro; it is independent of the
system’s internal judge, and its verdict on a request is never fed back
into the generation of that request.

##### Implementation details.

The generator is always frozen: Qwen-Image-2.0 for the main MindBench
results and the judge experiments
(§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")),
and Wan2.7-Image elsewhere. The internal judge scores each image along
five dimensions: Alignment, Faithfulness, Quality, Aesthetic, and
Physics
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2 "Verification and targeted repair. ‣ 3.2 Online Generation and Verification ‣ 3 Method ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).
An image is accepted if its weighted score is at least 4.5 and no veto
is triggered; otherwise, the system repairs the localized defects, using
zero, one, or two repair rounds per request. For each baseline, we
report the higher of our reproduction and the value claimed in its
original paper.

#### 4.1.2 Results on MindBench

As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1.2 Results on MindBench ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"),
ImageRSI achieves an overall CSA of 48.2%, outperforming all baselines.
It improves over direct generation with its own generator,
Qwen-Image-2.0 (22.4%), by 25.8 percentage points (pp), and over the
strongest agent baseline, GEMS [He et al. (2026c)](#bib.bib19)(42.4%),
by 5.8 pp; with Wan2.7-Image, ImageRSI reaches 47.4%. Per category,
ImageRSI ranks first on IP (30%) and leads most clearly on Math (80% vs.
46% for Nano Banana Pro).

Replacing the generator with Nano Banana Pro raises the overall CSA of
ImageRSI to 52.6% (263/500), 4.4 pp higher than the Qwen-Image-2.0
version; the difference comes mainly from SE (70% vs. 48%) and SL (72%
vs. 56%).

### 4.2 Effectiveness of Verification and Repair

We first test whether the gain from verification and repair comes only
from generating one additional image, by comparing second-round
strategies under the same generation budget.

##### Experimental settings.

The repair and experience-reuse ablations
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Effectiveness of Verification and Repair ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
and
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Experience Reuse ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"))
use the test set defined in
§[4.1.1](#S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1 "Benchmarks. ‣ 4.1.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"),
with Wan2.7-Image for generation and Gemini 3.1 Pro for evaluation.

##### Compared strategies.

All strategies share the same first-round image. If the judge accepts
it, the image is delivered directly; otherwise, one of the following
strategies generates a second image. Each request therefore receives at
most two images, and all strategies have the same generation budget. (i)
Best-of-2 resampling: regenerate with the same prompt and let the judge
select the better image; (ii) Generic-feedback repair: ask the rewriter
to revise the original prompt without specifying the defects; (iii)
Localized repair (ImageRSI): specify the localized defects in the
rewrite instruction and lock the parsed requirements
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1 "Requirement-preserving generation. ‣ 3.2 Online Generation and Verification ‣ 3 Method ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"))
so that satisfied requirements are preserved. We also ablate requirement
locking by removing it from localized repair, keeping all else
unchanged.

##### Results.

As shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results. ‣ 4.2 Effectiveness of Verification and Repair ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")a,
localized repair raises CSA from 53.4% to 65.7% (+12.3 pp), 10.7 pp
above Best-of-2 resampling, which gains only 1.6 pp. The gain therefore
does not come from the additional generation alone. Generic-feedback
repair gains only 3.2 pp, indicating that signaling failure alone is of
limited help. Without requirement locking, CSA drops to 57.8%, 7.9 pp
below full localized repair, suggesting that locking contributes
substantially to the gain.

Figure 3: Ablation studies of repair strategies and experience library
size on the held-out test set. (a) Second-round strategies with a shared
first-round image and at most two images per request; bars show the gain
over the first-round image only (pp), and labels give CSA (%) with the
gain. (b) CSA with nested experience libraries of 0, 131, 266, and 527
entries.

Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Results. ‣ 4.2 Effectiveness of Verification and Repair ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
presents two cases. Case (a) requires a desert roadside gas station to
display a complete, legible Shell emblem, comprising the scallop-shell
graphic and the brand name “Shell,” on both the canopy front and the
fuel-pump casing. In the first-round image, both emblems show only the
graphic without the text, failing the three text-related check items
(6/9); the judge correctly localizes the missing brand name. Case (b)
requires the main character to present measurement results to two
assistants in a radiation laboratory, with detailed constraints on her
appearance and clothing and on how the two assistants differ. In the
first-round image, she faces forward while operating an instrument,
without interacting with the assistants, who are also not standing
behind the instruments; two items fail (8/10), and the judge identifies
the missing interaction with the assistants. In both cases, the second
images from Best-of-2 resampling and generic-feedback repair fail to fix
these errors; in case (b), the generic-feedback image even contains
three assistants and loses two previously satisfied requirements (6/10).
Localized repair instead states the defect in the rewritten prompt and
excludes it in the negative prompt (“graphic only, no text”; “facing
forward and operating an instrument, no interaction”), after which all
items pass in both cases.

Figure 4: Verification-and-repair cases from the test set: (a) case

### 4.3 Experience Reuse

| ------------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------- |
| Internal judge                  | MAE $`\downarrow`$ | MindBench CSA (%) |
| Frozen closed-source models     |                    |                   |
| Qwen3.6-Plus                    | –                  | 24.2              |
| Qwen3.7-Plus                    | –                  | 43.4              |
| GPT-6-Astra                     | –                  | 44.2              |
| Qwen3.8-27B with judge training |                    |                   |
| Base (untrained)                | 0.598              | 38.6              |
| SFT\_(30%)                      | 0.596              | 39.8              |
| SFT\_(60%)                      | 0.582              | 40.2              |
| SFT\_(100%)                     | 0.453              | 44.8              |
| GRPO\_(100%)                    | 0.403              | 48.2              |

Table 3: End-to-end MindBench results with different internal judges.
Best values are in bold and second-best values are underlined. MAE is
computed against teacher scores on the same 90 images (–: not reported);
end-to-end runs use the Qwen-Image-2.0 generator, at most two repair
rounds, and a frozen experience library.

Beyond repairing a single request, ImageRSI reuses experience across
requests. We examine whether experience accumulated from past
trajectories improves performance on new requests, and whether the gain
grows with library size.

##### Experience construction and use.

Taking the final prompt delivered to the generator as the trajectory and
the external evaluator’s per-item verdicts as supervision, Qwen3.8-Max
distills one candidate experience per request in the experience set.
Each candidate specifies the applicable request type (with proper nouns,
numbers, and text content removed), at most three sentences of
prompt-writing advice, and the check items most prone to failure for
such requests. We retain 527 experiences after applying the admission
protocol in
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Experience Admission ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation").
At inference time, the system retrieves the three most similar
experiences by character-bigram TF-IDF similarity and injects them into
prompt rewriting in both the first round and the repair round; all other
settings follow localized repair in
§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Effectiveness of Verification and Repair ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation").

##### Library size.

We arrange the experience-set requests in a fixed random order and take
successive prefixes to build four nested libraries with 0, 131, 266, and
527 experiences, corresponding to roughly 0%, 25%, 50%, and 100% of the
full library. The libraries differ only in size.

##### Results.

As shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results. ‣ 4.2 Effectiveness of Verification and Repair ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")b,
CSA increases monotonically with library size: 55.7%, 56.8%, 61.3%, and
65.7%. The full library improves CSA by 10.0 pp over using no experience
and exceeds the 25% and 50% libraries by 8.8 and 4.4 pp, respectively.
The benefit of experience reuse thus grows with the size of the library.

### 4.4 Recursive Self-Improvement

ImageRSI improves itself at two levels. Within a task, it revises its
output round by round based on judge feedback; across tasks, it distills
trajectories into experience and updates the judge with accumulated
judgment records. This section evaluates the judge update
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Judger Self-Evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).

##### Setup.

We train Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 30%, 60%, and
100% of the SFT training set, obtaining SFT*(30%), SFT*(60%), and
SFT*(100%). We then train GRPO*(100%) with GRPO initialized from
SFT\_(100%) on a separate GRPO training set whose requests do not overlap
with the SFT set, keeping the SFT output format. The GRPO reward
combines pointwise assessment with within-group ranking
(Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Training Objective ‣ Appendix D Judge Training ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).
The pointwise term scores both the five-dimensional scores, through the
weighted scoring error and per-dimension agreement with the target label
at the pass boundary (score $`\geq 4`$), and the rationales, by checking
whether each criticism is supported by the image and the request.
Malformed outputs receive the lowest reward; accepting an image whose
target alignment or faithfulness score is at most 2, or making a
critical fabrication or omission, moves the reward into a separate lower
band that accurate assessments on other dimensions cannot offset. We
report the mean absolute error (MAE) against teacher-model reference
scores and the end-to-end CSA when each judge is plugged into the full
pipeline. For reference, we also report results with off-the-shelf
multimodal LLMs used as the internal judge without training.

##### Results.

As shown in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Experience Reuse ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"),
as the training data grows from 30% to 100%, the MAE of the SFT judges
decreases from 0.596 to 0.453 (base model: 0.598), and CSA increases
from 39.8% to 44.8% (base model: 38.6%). GRPO further reduces MAE to
0.403 and raises CSA to 48.2%, the best on both metrics, improving over
SFT\_(100%) by 0.050 and 3.4 pp, respectively. Off-the-shelf judges yield
CSA between 24.2% (Qwen3.6-Plus) and 44.2% (GPT-6-Astra), showing that
the choice of judge markedly affects system performance. Base model
without updates (38.6%) falls below Qwen3.7-Plus and GPT-6-Astra,
whereas after SFT and GRPO (48.2%) it surpasses all off-the-shelf
judges, exceeding GPT-6-Astra by 4.0 pp. Training on the system’s own
accumulated judgment records thus enables the 27B judge to outperform
every off-the-shelf judge we evaluated.

## 5 Conclusion

ImageRSI couples five-dimensional verification and targeted repair with
a validated cross-task experience library and offline judger
self-evolution under a frozen image generator. It reaches 52.6% CSA on
MindBench with Nano Banana Pro and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench. Under a
matched generation budget, localized repair with requirement locking
outperforms resampling and generic feedback, and CSA increases with the
size of the experience library; post-training the judge on accumulated
judgment records further improves end-to-end CSA. The gains from
repeated collection–training cycles remain to be evaluated.

## Limitations

We evaluate ImageRSI with several base image generators. Our focus is on
improving generation quality for a given generator through verification,
repair, and cross-task experience reuse. A related application arises
when the base generator is replaced. Here, existing experience could be
reused to reduce the cost of accumulating it again. For example, one
could study which experiences transfer directly and which need to be
adapted to the characteristics of the new generator. Such optimizations
could be added to the existing pipeline as an optional extension of the
experience library, and they are independent of the contributions of our
method.

## Appendix A Implementation Details

### A.1 Generation and Delivery

Retrieval is limited to four passes per request. Each round generates
one image, and a request receives an initial round followed by at most
two repair rounds; the direct-generation baseline uses a single round.
In each round, the workflow selects experience, builds the prompt from
the fixed requirements and earlier feedback, generates an image, and
scores it. The first accepted image is returned. If no round is accepted
within the budget, the highest-scoring judged image is returned as a
fallback; it is not counted as accepted. Failed generation or judging
calls are recorded in the trajectory.

### A.2 Scoring and Acceptance

Each dimension is scored on an integer scale from 1 to 5. For T2I
requests, the base weights of Alignment, Faithfulness, Quality,
Aesthetic, and Physics are $`0.40`$, $`0.20`$, $`0.25`$, $`0.20`$, and
$`0.15`$. Following
Equation [1](#S3.E1 "In Verification and targeted repair. ‣ 3.2 Online Generation and Verification ‣ 3 Method ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation"),
the weight of a low-confidence dimension is multiplied by $`0.7`$, and
the weights are then normalized over the active dimensions. I2I requests
additionally activate a reference-consistency check.

An image is accepted if its aggregate score is at least $`4.5`$ and no
veto applies. A Quality score of at most 3 vetoes acceptance; so does an
Alignment score of at most 3, unless the requirement parser reports low
confidence.

### A.3 Constraint-Aware Verification

In this optional variant, an extractor splits the request into atomic
requirements, each linked to its source phrase in the request. The
verifier labels every requirement pass, fail, or unknown and cites
visible evidence; counts that are occluded or relations that cannot be
seen remain unknown. Early acceptance requires every requirement to
pass. The repair prompt keeps the clauses of satisfied requirements and
rewrites only those for failed or unknown ones; satisfied requirements
are rechecked after repair.

### A.4 Experience Admission

A candidate needs at least two independent source trajectories. Each
validation trial applies only the candidate’s action, with the seed and
all upstream inputs shared between the two arms, and the image pair is
scored blind. Calibration and holdout use separate splits. Calibration
requires at least three trials, at least two positive differences
$`\Delta_{e}(q)`$, no negative difference, and a mean difference of at
least $`0.05`$. Holdout requires at least two trials, at least one
positive difference, no negative difference, and a nonnegative mean. A
candidate becomes verified after calibration and active after holdout;
any hard regression rejects it.

## Appendix B Datasets and Evaluation

### B.1 ImageReq-Bench

ImageReq-Bench is built around hard cases in real-world text-to-image
requests, i.e., requests whose requirements current generators often
fail to satisfy jointly. Benchmark scope and the experience/test split
are described in
§[4.1.1](#S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1 "Benchmarks. ‣ 4.1.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation").
During curation, we deduplicated candidate requests and removed or
replaced identified personal information. Each request is linked to its
source records. All methods and judges are evaluated on the same fixed
list of test case IDs.

We consolidate the 12 content categories into four: Illustration (511
requests), Scene (213), Infographic (144), and Design & Art (93). These
categories are organizational labels rather than a validated difficulty
taxonomy.

Language or vision–language models were used to draft and refine a
checklist for each request, removing unsupported requirements, merging
duplicate items, and expressing the remaining requirements as visually
checkable statements. Checklists contain 2 to 18 items per request, and
all methods are scored against the same checklist version. The benchmark
assesses whether multiple requirements within a request are jointly
satisfied and uses individual checks to identify unmet requirements,
providing a common basis for evaluating image generation, targeted
repair, and cross-task experience reuse.

The three MindBench I2I categories (Life, GU, and Math) comprise 150
requests.

### B.2 Checklist Strict Accuracy

Let $`b_{ij}`$ be the external evaluator’s Boolean verdict on checklist
item $`j`$ of request $`i`$. Request $`i`$ passes ($`y_{i}=1`$) only if
a delivered image exists, the evaluator returns a valid verdict for
every item, and all $`b_{ij}`$ are true; otherwise $`y_{i}=0`$. For an
evaluation set of $`N`$ requests,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \operatorname{CSA}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}y_{i}.
       ```                                                 |     | (3) |

Malformed evaluator responses are never parsed as passes.

The external evaluator, Gemini 3.1 Pro, is separate from the internal
judge. Its verdicts on a request are never fed back into the generation
of that request; experience is distilled only from verdicts on the
experience set
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Experience Reuse ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).

lists the fields of an experience record. During selection, the model
first sees only the Domain, Task Type, Generation Type, and Failure
Pattern of each entry, and then loads the selected entries in full.

| Field                              | Content                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Domain, Task Type, Generation Type | Subject area and input modality, used to narrow retrieval.                  |
| Failure Pattern, Trigger           | The observed failure or request condition under which the strategy applies. |
| Negative Trigger                   | Conditions under which the strategy should not be used.                     |
| Action, protected constraints      | The prompt change and the requirements it must keep.                        |
| Effect, Known Side Effects         | Observed outcomes in trials and possible regressions.                       |
| Source, trial records, state       | Supporting trajectories, paired validation trials, and admission state.     |

## Appendix D Judge Training

### D.1 Training Data

##### Training requests.

We assemble approximately 2,000 requests for judge training, combining
530 requests from the experience split of ImageReq-Bench with
approximately 1,500 additional requests. The latter are constructed
using WISE’s taxonomy and prompt design as guidance, together with
MindBench’s knowledge- and reasoning-driven task categories ([Niu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [He et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11)). WISE provides
sampled coverage of world knowledge, while MindBench contains 50
evaluation examples per category. Although both offer useful evaluation
resources, neither directly supplies the five-dimensional
score-and-reason supervision required by our judge. We therefore expand
the request pool along their task categories and pair selected images
from generation and repair trajectories with dimension-specific scores
and evidence-grounded explanations.

##### Inputs and targets.

Each training input contains the request, the parsed requirements,
permitted evidence, any task input image, and the generated image. The
target consists of five lines, one per dimension in the order Alignment,
Faithfulness, Quality, Physics, and Aesthetic; each line gives an
integer score from 1 to 5 and a reason grounded in the image. Images
that violate the request are kept, since their targets describe the
violation. Training covers only scores and reasons. The confidence
values used in
Equation [1](#S3.E1 "In Verification and targeted repair. ‣ 3.2 Online Generation and Verification ‣ 3 Method ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
are set to constants by an inference adapter when a trained judge is
deployed.

### D.2 Training Objective

Let $`z`$ be the judge input and $`y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{L})`$ the target
response. SFT minimizes

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\log p_{\theta}(y_{\ell}\mid z,y_{<\ell}),
``` |  | (4) |

with prompt and image tokens masked from the loss. GRPO then starts from
the SFT_(100%) checkpoint.

##### GRPO reward.

The GRPO reward combines pointwise assessment with within-group ranking.
Pointwise assessment evaluates five-dimensional score accuracy and
rationale correctness, checking whether the judge’s criticisms are
supported by the image and task requirements and identifying overly
harsh assessments or other misjudgments. Malformed outputs receive the
lowest reward, while severe false accepts and critical fabrications or
omissions enter a separate lower reward band that cannot be offset by
other dimensions. Within each band, a small ranking adjustment is added
only when two reversed-order reviews yield consistent,
evidence-supported rankings with sufficient confidence. Score
aggregation and acceptance rules are fixed and not learned.

## Appendix E Experimental Details

### E.1 Baselines on MindBench

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1.2 Results on MindBench ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
combines values reported in the original papers with our reproductions;
for each baseline, we report the higher of the two
(§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")).
GEMS and GenSearcher-style are reproduced locally with the
Qwen-Image-2.0 generator and a Gemini 3.1 Pro backbone; image retrieval
is unavailable in our GenSearcher-style reproduction. Seedream 4.5 is
evaluated with direct generation. Wan2.7-Image is run locally; one
request remained unevaluated and is counted as a failure, so its CSA is
a lower bound. For ImageRSI (Nano Banana Pro), 12 requests produced no
image and are counted as failures.

### E.2 Repair Strategies

In generic-feedback repair, the rewriter is told only that the image did
not pass and is asked to improve the prompt against the original
request; no defect information is given.
Table [5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ E.2 Repair Strategies ‣ Appendix E Experimental Details ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")

Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Results. ‣ 4.2 Effectiveness of Verification and Repair ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation")
use seeds 12345 (case 1006) and 22345 (case 0656).

reports an offline ablation of the judge’s score aggregation.

Figure 5: Offline ablation of the five-dimensional judge on delivered
ImageReq-Bench images. Each point re-aggregates the recorded dimension
scores under one configuration and compares the resulting decision with
the external CSA label. Removing the alignment dimension raises the
false-accept rate from 24.8% to 37.1%; removing the quality dimension or
the hard vetoes increases recall but also the false-accept rate;
removing the low-confidence discount changes no decision and thus
coincides with the deployed configuration. “w/o aesth./faith.” marks the
